transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

I came in because I can’t stop thinking about how the left side of my face looks. My nose and jaw seem crooked, especially in ID photos or on the online class camera. People tell me they don’t see it, but I feel like everyone in the CNC lab notices it before they notice my work.
On an average day, roughly how many hours do you spend thinking about or checking the appearance of your face?

A few hours, probably. Before school I can get stuck in the mirror or using my phone camera, trying to fix my hair or changing shirts so my face doesn’t look as bad. I’ll ask my mom if it looks weird too. Sometimes it takes so long I miss lab or get there too exhausted to focus.

When people tell you your face doesn't look crooked, do you think it's possible they're right and you might be misjudging your appearance, or do you feel completely certain that your face really is asymmetrical no matter what anyone says?

I mean, I hear them, but I don’t really believe it. In photos and on the class camera, the left side looks clearly off to me—my nose and jaw look crooked. It feels like people in the lab notice it right away, even if they say they don’t.

Aside from concerns about your face, have you noticed any other unusual experiences lately—like feeling that people are watching or talking about you, hearing things others don't, or having other beliefs that people around you find hard to understand?
No, I haven’t had anything like that. It’s mostly just the worry about how my face looks and whether people notice it.

Besides checking your face in the mirror or camera, do you also find yourself frequently comparing your face to other people's faces, or trying to hide or camouflage the 'crooked' side—like with hair, makeup, or head positioning—throughout the day?

Yeah. I keep checking the mirror and my phone camera before I leave, trying to get my hair right or changing shirts so the angle doesn’t show as much. I’ll ask my mom if it looks weird too. It can take so long that I miss lab or get there too exhausted to focus.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a preoccupation with a perceived defect in facial symmetry (nose and jaw appearing crooked) that is not observable or appears only slight to others. This preoccupation is associated with repetitive behaviors (mirror checking, camera checking, camouflaging with hair/clothing, seeking reassurance from mother) and is time-consuming (several hours/day), causing functional impairment (missing lab, exhaustion affecting academic performance). The patient shows poor insight/near-delusional conviction (does not believe others despite their reassurance) but denies other psychotic symptoms (no paranoia, hallucinations, or bizarre beliefs), making a primary psychotic disorder (F22.0) less likely. The circumscribed nature of the belief (limited to appearance) and absence of broader delusional content support BDD with absent insight/delusional beliefs specifier rather than a psychotic disorder.
